findings.title: BatchNFTMinter wired to V1 ITokenMinter interface; non-functional against production NFTMinterV2
findings.rootCause: BatchNFTMinter imports legacy V1 ITokenMinter and calls 3-arg mint(address,uint256,address). Production NFTMinterV2 only exposes mint(uint256,address) and mint(uint256,address,bytes). Selectors differ; every batchMint reverts on selector miss against the V2 minter. MockITokenMinter mirrors V1 so the test suite does not catch the regression.
findings.impact: Functional DoS of the entire helper against the spec-bound production minter. Users lose gas; the documented UX optimisation is undelivered.
findings.recommendation: Re-target BatchNFTMinter at ITokenMinterV2 (`yield-claim-nft/V2/interfaces/ITokenMinterV2.sol`) and call `mint(dispatcherIndex, recipient)`. Add an integration test against the deployed NFTMinterV2 ABI rather than the V1 mock.
findings.dedupNotes: No code-scanner counterpart; econ-scanner uniquely caught the V1/V2 selector mismatch. Strongest finding in the set; should anchor the submission.

findings.title: batchMint has no per-mint or cumulative price ceiling; front-runner can bump price between submission and inclusion, gas-griefing the entire batch
findings.rootCause: No `maxStartingPrice` / `maxCumulativePrice` parameter. Dispatcher's `price` grows by `growthBasisPoints` per mint; any concurrent mint between user submission and inclusion makes the cumulative cost exceed the prepaid `paymentAmount`, reverting the entire batch atomically.
findings.impact: Honest batch minters lose gas on reverted batches. Front-runner secures the cheapest slots and the early-minter geometric APY premium (compounds with DEDUP-006). Atomic rollback prevents overpayment but does not prevent denial.
findings.recommendation: Add a `maxCumulativePrice` (or `maxPerMintPrice`) parameter and revert if `nftMinter.configs(dispatcherIndex).price > maxStartingPrice` at the start of the call. A coarse `maxPaymentPerMint` would also bound user downside.
findings.dedupNotes: Distinct from DEDUP-003 (which is dispatcher-leg AMM slippage on the Balancer pool). DEDUP-002 is curve-side price growth between blocks; DEDUP-003 is in-block AMM slippage during the swap leg. Different root causes, different mitigations — both kept.

findings.title: batchMint forfeits dispatcher-side slippage protection by passing empty extraData on every iteration
findings.rootCause: BatchNFTMinter calls the no-extraData overload of `ITokenMinter.mint`. The interface natspec documents `extraData` as dispatcher-specific slippage parameters. The BalancerPooler dispatcher routes payment through a Balancer pool swap; without slippage params the swap accepts whatever the pool quotes at execution time. Single-mint callers can pick the extraData overload; batch callers cannot.
findings.impact: MEV searchers can sandwich every batch mint on the Balancer leg. The aggregate `paymentAmount` upfront pull bounds caller loss only by the dispatcher's revert-on-insufficient-balance; for batches large enough to move the pool the loss can dwarf per-iteration price growth.
findings.recommendation: Add an `extraData` (single shared) or `bytes[] calldata extraDatas` (per-iteration) parameter to `batchMint` and forward to the slippage-aware mint overload.
findings.dedupNotes: Sibling of DEDUP-002 but addresses a different leg of the price-execution path (in-block AMM swap vs cross-block price-curve growth). Independent mitigations required.

findings.title: batchMint pre-approves nftMinter for type(uint256).max for the entire loop, exposing the full paymentAmount to the configured dispatcher
findings.rootCause: Allowance is set to `type(uint256).max` before the loop and revoked only after it ends. For the loop's duration the dispatcher (or any callback path it triggers) has authority to pull the contract's full balance rather than the metered per-mint `price`. The contract also explicitly omits ReentrancyGuard.
findings.impact: Caller's full `paymentAmount` is at risk if a registered dispatcher turns hostile, has a callback bug, or invokes a token hook that re-enters. Today's BalancerPoolerV2 dispatcher does not callback to msg.sender, so the surface is latent — but the trust amplification vs. an N-call single-mint sequence is structural.
findings.recommendation: Replace the max approval with `paymentToken.forceApprove(address(nftMinter), paymentAmount)` (single-line change — bounds dispatcher authority by what the user already authorised). Optionally approve per-iteration with `nftMinter.getPrice(dispatcherIndex)` for an even tighter window. Update the L29 docstring claim about omitted reentrancy guards if approach changes.
findings.dedupNotes: MERGED CODE-BNM-002 + ECON-003. Same root cause (max approval held across entire loop). CODE framed as drain authority by the dispatcher; ECON framed as reentrancy-callback surface combined with omitted nonReentrant. Both reach the same `approve(paymentAmount)` recommendation. Combined framing is stronger than either alone.

findings.title: BatchNFTMinter collapses multi-tx mint cadence into a single transaction, simultaneously amplifying L-04 runway depletion and concentrating the early-minter geometric APY premium
findings.rootCause: A single `batchMint(count=N)` produces `latestPrice * (1 + g)^N` and accumulates `mintDebt` for N mints atomically. This (a) accelerates NFTStaker runway depletion via the next `_recomputeSchedule` (prior-audit L-04 amplification — the multi-tx cadence assumption that operators may have implicitly relied on collapses to a single tx), and (b) lets a single first-batch attacker capture the entire geometric APY premium pool (`r^N + r^(N-1) + ... + r^1`) before any organic minters can compete for the early slots. Without batching, each mint is a separate mempool event and competing minters can front-run each other for early slots.
findings.impact:
Two-axis impact:
  - Runway: operators counting on inter-mint reaction windows lose them; a single tx can collapse `windowEnd` measurably.
  - Distribution: first batch minter earns several multiples of `targetAPY` (per ECON-005's worked example: `targetAPY * r^N` ≈ 3.4x targetAPY for N=100, r=1.025) for the lifetime of their stake, paid for by later organic stakers' mintDebt. Reward budget drains faster than baseline organic-distribution scenarios assume.
findings.recommendation: Cap `count` per `batchMint` invocation (e.g. MAX_BATCH = 10 or 32) so that wholesale early-minter capture requires multiple separate transactions, restoring some of the front-running competition the original design assumed. Stronger fix: per-block / per-tx mint-rate limit at the NFTMinterV2 dispatcher layer that batched calls cannot bypass. Document the runway-stability implication in BatchNFTMinter natspec so operators size buffers accordingly.
findings.dedupNotes: MERGED CODE-BNM-006 + ECON-005 + ECON-006. All three trace to the same enabler (atomic N mints in 1 tx). CODE-BNM-006 captured the L-04 runway-depletion angle; ECON-005 captured the early-minter premium concentration angle; ECON-006 captured the mintDebt-inflation angle (which ECON-006 itself concludes is only profitable 'when combined with ECON-005'). Merging produces a single cohesive mechanism finding with stronger framing on all three vectors. Same root mitigation (cap count or rate-limit at dispatcher) addresses all three.

findings.title: M-03 staked-subset notional `S = totalStaked * latestPrice` uses bare multiplication; safe for documented param envelope but unprotected against future high-supply / high-price configs
findings.rootCause: Bare `totalStaked * latestPrice` with no overflow guard. Natspec bounds the product at ~1e27 under current params, but `totalStaked` is not enforced on-chain and a future stakedId rotation to a higher-supply token combined with sustained `growthBasisPoints` mints can push past 2^256.
findings.impact: Currently no exploitable path. If parameters drift outside the documented envelope, Solidity 0.8 checked arithmetic catches the overflow as a revert in `_recomputeSchedule`, DoS-ing every interaction (stake / unstake / claim / topUp / setTargetAPY / setDispatcherIndex / setNFTMinter / pullAndRefresh) until `emergencyWithdraw` reduces totalStaked. Solvency invariant is preserved (principal recoverable via emergencyWithdraw).
findings.recommendation: Cheapest defensive hardening: `require(latestPrice == 0 || totalStaked <= type(uint256).max / latestPrice, NFTStaker__SOverflow())` before the bare mul, with a typed error so monitoring can react before total interaction DoS sets in.
findings.dedupNotes: No econ-scanner counterpart (econ-scanner instead verified M-03 fix robustness from the participation-multiplier angle and explicitly concluded ROBUST). The overflow concern is orthogonal to participation correctness — kept as the only mechanical hardening item on the NFTStaker M-03 code path.

findings.title: totalPaid return value reports 0 when caller actually spent paymentAmount and received an unrelated donation refund as a windfall
findings.rootCause: When a third-party donation pre-loads the contract balance, `remaining > paymentAmount` after the loop. The clamp `paymentAmount > remaining ? paymentAmount - remaining : 0` returns `totalPaid = 0` even though the dispatcher pulled real cost. Off-chain accounting treats a paid mint as free.
findings.impact: Off-chain integrator accounting bug. No on-chain asset loss — caller's wallet flow is internally consistent (paid dispatcher, received donation as refund, net wallet correct). Only the helper's `totalPaid` return value is wrong.
findings.recommendation: Either snapshot pre-call balance and compute `totalPaid = paymentAmount + preBal > remaining ? paymentAmount + preBal - remaining : 0`, OR document in natspec that `totalPaid == 0` does not imply zero-cost mint when donations are present.
findings.dedupNotes: Adjacent to ECON-008 (donor-windfall MEV race) but different root cause: ECON-008 is about who captures the donation; DEDUP-007 is about the return value being wrong for the user who legitimately paid. Kept separately because the mitigations differ (snapshot pre-balance vs restrict refund recipient).

findings.title: Pre-deposited payment-token donations to BatchNFTMinter accrue to the next caller; an MEV bot can sweep donor windfalls
findings.rootCause: Documented behavior: any payment-token balance left on the contract flows to whoever calls batchMint next. Confused users who transfer payment-token directly to BatchNFTMinter (instead of approving + calling) cannot recover their funds; an MEV bot watching for such deposits captures them via a `count=1, paymentAmount=0` call.
findings.impact: Donors lose funds with no recovery; MEV operators win against organic users who might otherwise have benefited from the next-caller-wins design. Documented intentional behavior, but still constitutes a user-loss trap.
findings.recommendation: Conservative: record `lastFunder` (msg.sender of the most recent paymentAmount > 0 call) and refund residual to that address rather than the current caller. Minimal: add a clear user-facing warning in docs not to send tokens directly to BatchNFTMinter.
findings.dedupNotes: Borderline — could be classed as 'documented intentional design' and dropped. Kept as a low because it has a concrete user-loss path (donor) distinct from the merely-stylistic items dropped below. Distinct from DEDUP-007 (which is a return-value bug, not a fund flow).

mergedPairs.rationale: Same root cause (max approval held for entire loop duration). Code-scanner framed as 'dispatcher drain authority during loop'; econ-scanner framed as 'unbounded approval window combined with no nonReentrant guard'. Both findings reach the same one-line fix: replace `forceApprove(max)` with `forceApprove(paymentAmount)`. Combined framing covers both the dispatcher-trust angle and the reentrancy-callback angle without duplication.

All three findings exploit the same enabler — `batchMint` collapsing N sequential mint txs into a single atomic tx. CODE-BNM-006 traced the L-04 runway-depletion amplification angle; ECON-005 traced the early-minter geometric premium concentration; ECON-006 traced mintDebt feedback (and explicitly self-noted it is only profitable when combined with ECON-005). Single mitigation (cap `count`, or per-block mint rate limit at dispatcher) addresses all three impacts. Merging into one mechanism finding produces the strongest framing — economic distortion + runway acceleration + view inflation, all from one design surface.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: batchMint ignores nftMinter.mint() bool return value
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: Latent risk only. Code-scanner itself notes the only known implementation reverts on failure ('None today'). Generic unchecked-return-value pattern that adds no unique insight; below the C4 quality bar for HM submission and would dilute the QA report. If the protocol later adopts a non-reverting implementation, the issue can be re-flagged.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: Caller-controlled count has no upper bound (OOG self-grief)
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: Code-scanner self-classifies as 'Self-inflicted gas burn. UX gotcha, not a vulnerability.' No protocol asset risk, only caller's own gas. Common-pattern finding any tool would surface; falls into the C4 known-invalid bucket of 'user input mistakes'.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: Fee-on-transfer payment-token incompatibility (totalPaid mis-accounted)
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: C4 known-invalid finding: 'Fee-on-transfer tokens (unless explicitly in scope)'. Code-scanner already flags this is QA-only and the dispatcher leg is FOT-safe. Drops cleanly per the project's C4 scope rules.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: ScheduleRecomputed event field name retained despite semantics drift (M-03)
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: Already self-flagged in the raw scan as `intentionalDesign: true` and `noActionRequired: true`. Project's pre-existing-design-decisions list explicitly preserves the field name for off-chain consumer compat. Excluded per the scopeNotes 'pre-existing intentional-design items intentionally NOT re-flagged'.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: Unconstrained recipient — minting to NFTStaker burns the NFTs
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: C4 known-invalid: 'User input mistakes / phishing'. Econ-scanner itself classifies as 'naive users following bad docs / phishing UIs'. Standard user-error trap with documented mitigation (don't send directly); does not meet HM bar.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: BatchNFTMinter emits no events (observability gap)
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: Pure observability / informational. Econ-scanner self-classifies as 'observability gap, not a vulnerability'. C4 explicitly discourages 'missing event emissions' as QA-at-best; not a survivable submission.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: DUST_THRESHOLD check uses `remaining / DUST_THRESHOLD != 0` style
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: Pure code-style nit. Econ-scanner self-classifies as 'economic-impact zero today; maintainability risk only'. Style issue vs security concern per dedup policy.

commonOrLowValueDrops.title: BatchNFTMinter inflates mintDebt; pullAndRefresh sandwich gated by owner
commonOrLowValueDrops.dropRationale: MERGED into DEDUP-005 rather than a standalone drop. Econ-scanner itself concludes 'not profitable as a standalone attack; only profitable when combined with the ECON-005 geometric premium capture' and reaches 'No code change needed' for the standalone view. The mintDebt-inflation observation is folded into DEDUP-005's runway / distribution amplification framing.

topPriorities: DEDUP-001 (high) — V1/V2 interface mismatch; helper is dead-on-arrival against production minter
DEDUP-005 (medium) — batch collapses mint cadence into single tx, amplifying L-04 runway depletion and concentrating early-minter geometric APY premium
DEDUP-002 (medium) — no maxPrice ceiling enables sandwich-grief reverts
DEDUP-003 (medium) — no extraData forwarding forfeits Balancer-leg slippage protection
